title: Signet Jewelers Repositions H. Samuel And Ernest Jones Within The Watch Market
text: It has been a rollercoaster six years since Neil Old took the reins as managing director of Signet Jewelers’ UK business, which operates national jewellery chains H. Samuel and Ernest Jones. Starting in 2019, he almost immediately had to close every showroom because of the pandemic. Two years later war in Ukraine broke out. Since then, successive governments have ignored the needs of a squeezed retail sector and piled on extra costs through hikes to the National Living Wage, higher taxes and new regulations. But every crisis is an opportunity, and the Signet team has been diligently repositioning its UK watch business, pivoting Ernest Jones away from an increasingly unattainable luxury segment and into a more commercially viable mid-market. The group has exited what it calls “prestige watch” retailing for brands including Omega, Cartier, IWC and Panerai, after concluding that, without access to Rolex and other dominant names, it could not compete sustainably at the top end. In its place, Ernest Jones is being reshaped around a clearer, more focused proposition: a “premier” watch segment spanning roughly £600 to £1,500, featuring brands such as Longines, Tissot and Rado. This positions the chain above H. Samuel while still remaining accessible to a broader customer base. Crucially, average selling prices at Ernest Jones are now around double those at H. Samuel, underlining a deliberate segmentation between the two fascias in both pricing and target audience. Alongside this strategic shift, Signet has committed to upgrading both its store estate and digital platforms. Investment has already transformed large parts of the H. Samuel network, with a similar programme now beginning at Ernest Jones, aimed at delivering a more premium, differentiated retail experience both in-store and online. It is work in progress with a clear focus and agreed destination, Mr Old describes in this wide-ranging interview with WatchPro founder Rob Corder. Interview with Neil Old, managing director, Signet Jewelers UK H. Samuel’s refurbished store in Leeds. WP: Signet Jewelers is a publicly-traded company, so we can see the group’s financial results in the USA and UK, but how would you describe the performance over recent years, particularly since the pandemic? NO: I joined just before COVID in September 2019 when the company was undergoing its Path to Brilliance strategy. My remit was to come into the UK business and see how that strategy could be tailored for this market. It covered everything from the portfolio of stores we had, the services, product and brand portfolio and digital capability. Five months later we were hit by COVID, and in many respects that gave us the opportunity to accelerate what was going to be a three-year plan. Part of that was dealing with the fact that we had too many stores at the time, and we set about rightsizing the estate. Another focus was to dramatically accelerate improvements for our digital capabilities. Overnight, we became an ecommerce-only retailer because the 400 plus stores we had at the time were all shuttered. When lockdowns eased, we did not reopen every store but we kept and redeployed our very best people. This allowed us to build a tighter, more efficient estate, strengthen our digital capabilities, and bring together a highly skilled team. Since then, we have continued to refine our estate of stores and we have re-platformed our web business so we are running from the same system as Signet Group – a significant undertaking but improved the customer experience. The additional part of the plan for the UK market was to exit what we would call the luxury watch market, where at the top end we were dealing in brands like Cartier, Breitling and Omega. I took a critical look at the watch market and our position within it. We performed well in the 18 months following COVID, but as conditions normalised, it became clear that our long-term opportunities to re‑establish ourselves at the very top end of the market were limited. Watches of Switzerland Group was gaining watch sales by building Rolex space, particularly with Goldsmiths in locations where we were competing with Ernest Jones. Over time, it became evident that these highly competitive locations required significant effort to maintain sales, with limited prospects for sustainable growth. Seventy-seven percent of the watch market in this country is just six brands, within which Rolex is by far the largest. We asked ourselves whether we could compete in that space without those brands while at the same time recognising that we have two great brands of our own: H. Samuel and Ernest Jones. In H Samuel, we are strongest with slightly younger, perhaps more value-oriented customers, while Ernest Jones is well-established in the mid-market, which I came to view as somewhat overlooked and underserved. Internally, I might call it the premier watch market: Longines, Tissot, Rado, Gucci, with prices in the region of £600 to £800. WP: That is certainly a price point that many Swiss manufacturers have vacated. NO: A story I have shared a number of times with Swiss manufacturers and my team is about when my mother wanted to buy a really nice luxury watch for my father when he turned 70. I asked what she wanted to spend and she said she wanted to make it something really special, which to her was a budget of £600. That stuck with me when we have been discussing the market for even entry level luxury watches that now cost £3000 or £5000. WP: I agree your mother’s experience is a reality for 99% of watch customers, and you are right that we all give far too much attention to the needs of the 1%. NO: I decided we could stay on the hamster wheel chasing the luxury brands and join the space race with Watches of Switzerland Group opening monobrand and multibrand stores, or we could choose a different direction. A few years ago I met with Craig Bolton [UK president of Watches of Switzerland Group], who I already knew, at an event. We started talking about a deal to sell a number of Ernest Jones stores that were strongest in the luxury watch space. In 2023, we reached an agreement to sell 19 Ernest Jones stores: 14 multibrand showrooms and five monobrand boutiques. Some of the boutiques were taken back after that deal, including a few Omega stores that the brand decided to run themselves. We also had the Montblanc, IWC, Panerai and Jaeger-LeCoultre boutiques in Leeds which we continued to run for Richemont until recently. WP: How did you come to open those boutiques in the first place? NO: Richemont came to us and said they wanted to open boutiques outside London. We are stronger outside of London, which may be why they approached us. WP: That is interesting. I have written many times that Richemont has been too London-centric, but Leeds was one of the few places where its brands were well-represented by Berry’s. NO: We were not just talking about Leeds, but also other major UK cities. Leeds just happened to be first. It was an opportunity to grow with Richemont, particularly IWC, while continuing to strengthen our longstanding relationship with Cartier. The proposal was compelling and aligned with our strategic direction. Following the opening of the boutiques, a slowdown in the luxury watch market prompted a reassessment of their long‑term fit within the business. We continued to operate the stores for a period, but over time it became clear that they no longer aligned with our core focus. When a break clause in the agreement became available, it provided a practical opportunity to exit, which was the right decision for the business. Ernest Jones’ new digital storefront. WP: How does exiting the prestige watch market impact Ernest Jones and H. Samuel? When I look at the brand line up for both businesses, they are pretty similar today. NO: We do have many of the same brands, but the assortments of watches is quite different. Ernest Jones is focused more on the premium collections. Take a brand like Citizen, for example, they have quite different products that fit with an H. Samuel or an Ernest Jones customer. That makes them a great partner for us. The average selling price for a watch in Ernest Jones is double that of H. Samuel, so while the brand lineup looks similar, the offering is very clearly positioned. Sixty percent of our sales in H. Samuel come from what you might call the volume end of the market while at the same time half of the sales in Ernest Jones come from the premier end. We have clearly delineated rules of engagement. H. Samuel was always doing very well. It sells around one in four volume watches on the high street today and brings a lot of newness to market. That is very important to the industry as a whole. Before joining Signet, I used to work for Jessop with Peter Jones, who you will know from the BBC’s Dragons’ Den. He always used to say you can often see a gap in the market, but is there a market in the gap? What we had to do with Ernest Jones was to come up with something distinct from H. Samuel. We needed to find a gap in the market and a market in the gap, which is why we now have a clear focus on the £600 to £1,000 watch segment, which is above H. Samuel, but less expensive and with much higher potential volumes than retailers like Watches of Switzerland and Goldsmiths. That has really helped us to grow. When I look at our performance, the mix of sales today [watches versus jewellery] across our retail brands, is the same today as it was when we were still in the prestige business. It is not the case that watches are less important to us today, we just sell watches in greater volume because they are the correct fit for customers that come into H. Samuel and Ernest Jones’ stores. WP: Is H. Samuel a simpler business with greater potential than Ernest Jones in the current climate? I would say that £600 to £1000 is still a lot of money for people being squeezed by inflation and other financial pressures. NO: H. Samuel has performed better than Ernest Jones in recent years. When I joined, H. Samuel and Ernest Jones had not had store investment in a very long time. We opened a couple of major refits, the first in Milton Keynes, and we were delighted with the results. Since then, we have refined our approach to these refits and identified what really makes a difference to customers. With c170 H. Samuel stores, we need to be careful about investing in the right way making sure that any solution is scalable across such a large estate. Today, we see around 60% of H. Samuel sales coming from stores that have had investment over the past three years. These have generally been the stores in the best locations that were already performing well. As I mentioned earlier, we invested heavily in our ecommerce during COVID, but the experience in stores did not nearly match the quality we were delivering online. We were setting expectations high with a great digital experience across web, social media, customer emails, etc, but people would come into our stores and find them looking quite tired. Now, we have these brand-enhancing experiences in 60% of our stores and we are seeing younger people coming in, average prices rising and new categories succeeding. We prioritised investment in H. Samuel because it was playing and winning in a less congested part of the market. We have another full year of investment going into H. Samuel in 2026, but we are also slowly turning our attention to Ernest Jones. That will position the two brands even more distinctly. WP: Are there plans for an Ernest Jones flagship, where you put a stake in the ground and say, this is what we are all about? NO: We are now at the point where we are very open minded to new space. When we sold Ernest Jones stores to Watches of Switzerland, they were good stores and that left holes in our portfolio in key locations. If we can find the right deals in some of those locations, and we were very clear about the Ernest Jones proposition, that could be an option. WP: Signet Jewelers in the United States, with its Jared, Kay and Zales retail brands, are barely in watches at all. Do they get it when you discuss the direction for H. Samuel and Ernest Jones? NO: Our brands are involved in watches in the U.S., albeit to a smaller scale. Our CEO JK Symancyk recently noted that timepieces actually did quite well over the peak Christmas period. J.K. came on as CEO and we embarked on a new strategy: Grow Brand Love. One of the pillars for the strategy is delivering captivating experiences, and watches offer that. Ernest Jones in Leeds. WP: It is interesting when you look at the price points you are focused on with both H. Samuel and Ernest Jones, the Japanese manufacturers are killing it right now, both in the sub-£500 and over-£500 market. You only have to look at their financial results, which have been far better than for publicly-traded Swiss watchmaking groups over the past two years. I also think the likes of Citizen, Seiko and Casio are more agile and on-trend in their product development. All the action seems to be with these Japanese makers, and also independents like Christopher Ward, Studio Underd0g, Dennison, Fears, Formex, etc. If I was going to focus on the top six brands in the £500 to £1,500 space right now, I think three of them would be Japanese, and only a couple like Longines and Tissot would be Swiss. NO: I would add Rado to Longines and Tissot. But Citizen is one of our biggest partners. We have had double-digit growth with them this year. If I look at winners and losers in GfK data I see Citizen, Seiko and Sekonda up, and with each of these, our sales are up by more than the brands. That makes us an increasingly important partner to them. Garmin has also been great for us; it’s an incredible partner with product that fits very well for both Ernest Jones or H. Samuel. So, you are absolutely right. The Japanese brands and Garmin have been fantastic for us over the past 18 months. When I talk about the investment programme ahead of us, these brands are a key part of that. WP: Timex and Fossil Group are also interesting, and the American connection might play well with your HQ. NO: I noted Watches of Switzerland’s decision to partner with Timex, which shows the market is constantly changing and we have to be alive and agile to every opportunity. Watches of Switzerland acquisition of Ernest Jones stores generates $53 million for Signet Jewelers WP: The buying journey for customers, particularly in the luxury space, is often said to require about 10 touch points before a purchase is made, but whether that journey starts online or on social media, it almost always ends up on a store. Ecommerce in the luxury watch market is still under 10% of the total. How would you describe the same process in the volume game? NO: It is not the same, although it does depend on the time of year. Ahead of Christmas, for example, there are a lot more impulse buys, particularly with H. Samuel. Gifting is different to self-purchasing. Overall, it would be far fewer touch points leading up to a sale for H. Samuel. Also depending on the time of year, around one fifth to one quarter of our sales come from online. Watches typically over-index that, particularly at H. Samuel. WP: Do you expect to maintain a broad range of brands across your stores or, as we see in the luxury market, you will end up with far fewer brands being given much greater prominence? NO: We want to offer choice but we will also back our winners, like Citizen, at the moment. We will invest with them as they invest with us. Where I can see a very clear plan, as we do with the Japanese brands, I can see a very clear growth path ahead. Signet Jewelers opened the Leeds Panerai boutique in 2023, but it closed in November 2025. WP: There is a lot of talk about government decisions that have added costs for large retail businesses like yours. What is your view? NO: Like many large retailers, we continue to manage the impact of broader structural cost changes while remaining committed to investing in our colleagues who are fundamental to everything we achieve.
